title: Retail Replacement Sourcing
name: Retail Replacement Sourcing
metaTitle: Retail Replacement Sourcing in Phoenix, AZ
metaDescription: Sourcing grocery-anchored and neighborhood retail centers across metro Phoenix for 1031 exchange investors replacing multi-tenant retail property.

sections.html: Multi-tenant retail is a different search than a single net lease pad. You're underwriting a tenant mix, not one lease, and Phoenix has a wide range of it depending on which ring of the metro you're looking at.

sections.heading: Where Grocery-Anchored Centers Are Getting Built
sections.html: New grocery-anchored centers keep following the rooftops into Goodyear, Buckeye, and Surprise, timed to open alongside the apartment and single-family growth out there. Older centers in central Phoenix, Glendale, and Mesa trade on a different story: established trade areas with decades of sales history but tenant mixes that sometimes need repositioning.

sections.heading: Reading the Tenant Mix Beyond the Anchor
sections.html:
An anchor grocery tenant tells you the center draws traffic, but the shop tenants around it tell you whether that traffic turns into rent growth. We look at co-tenancy clauses tied to the anchor, since some smaller tenants can reduce rent or exit if the anchor closes, and we check how much of the center's income depends on one or two shop tenants.

Shop tenant categories matter too. A center with a mix of service tenants, salons, medical, financial, tends to hold occupancy better through retail slowdowns than a center leaning heavily on discretionary retail. We map the whole shop tenant mix before recommending a center, well beyond the anchor lease alone.

sections.heading: The Screen We Run on Every Retail Center
sections.html:
Before a retail center goes on your candidate list, it clears this checklist:

  • Anchor tenant sales history or, at minimum, lease strength and remaining term
  • Co-tenancy clauses that could trigger rent reductions
  • Vacancy and tenant turnover over the trailing two years
  • Deferred maintenance on roof, parking lot, and site lighting
  • Competing centers permitted or under construction within the trade area

That last item matters more in Phoenix's growth corridors than in the older core, since new supply can arrive fast where land is still available.

sections.heading: Fitting Retail Sourcing to Your Timeline
sections.html:
Retail center diligence generally takes longer than a single net lease pad because you're underwriting multiple leases and tenant relationships. We start building your candidate list before your relinquished property closes so the forty-five-day identification window isn't spent doing work that should already be done.

We source and underwrite; we don't give tax advice. If the retail center you like carries a lower price or debt load than what you sold, have your CPA check whether that creates boot before you identify it.

sections.heading: What Trips Investors Up on Retail
sections.html:
The most common mistake is underwriting the anchor and skipping the shop tenants. A center can look fully leased on paper while several shop spaces are on short-term leases at below-market rent, which changes the real income picture the day those leases come up for renewal.

A second mistake is underestimating how fast new competing retail can get built in Phoenix's growth submarkets. A center that looks like the only grocery-anchored option in a trade area today can have a competitor breaking ground within a year if the rooftops keep coming, so we check permitted projects before calling any trade area underserved.

sections.heading: How Financing Differs From Single-Tenant Retail
sections.html: Lenders generally look harder at a multi-tenant retail center than a single net lease pad, since the income stream depends on several leases rather than one. Anchor tenant strength, lease term stack, and historical occupancy all factor into how a lender sizes the loan. We flag likely financing terms on a candidate center early, so the identification decision accounts for how the debt side is actually going to underwrite.

sections.heading: A Real Retail Candidate We've Underwritten
sections.html: On one candidate in the West Valley, a grocery-anchored center looked fully leased at first glance, but the shop tenant roster showed three suites on short-term extensions rather than renewed leases. The anchor's remaining term and sales history were solid, but that shop tenant risk changed how we ranked the property against a competing center in Chandler with a smaller anchor but a fully renewed shop tenant lineup. The Chandler center ended up being the stronger long-term hold once we weighed both factors together.

sections.heading: Parking, Signage, and Access Details We Verify
sections.html: Retail centers live and die on how easy they are to reach and how visible each shop is from the parking field. We walk the site plan for shared parking ratios, pylon signage rights, and any cross-access easements with neighboring parcels before recommending a center, since disputes over any of those three can quietly erode value that the financials alone won't show.

faqs.q: What's different about sourcing a retail center versus a single net lease pad?
faqs.a: A center means underwriting an entire tenant mix, co-tenancy clauses, and vacancy history rather than a single lease. It takes more diligence time, which is why we start the search early.

faqs.q: Why do co-tenancy clauses matter when replacing anchored retail?
faqs.a: Some shop leases let the tenant reduce rent or exit if the anchor tenant closes. We check those clauses before recommending a center so you know the real downside risk.

faqs.q: How much new retail supply is coming to Phoenix's growth submarkets?
faqs.a: Grocery-anchored development is following the same rooftops growth pushing into Goodyear, Buckeye, and Surprise. We check permitted competing centers within the trade area before you identify a property.

faqs.q: Can a retail center with vacant shop space still work as a 1031 replacement?
faqs.a: It can, depending on your risk tolerance and the rest of the center's income. We show you the real vacancy and turnover history so that's a decision made with full information.

faqs.q: How far back do you check vacancy and turnover on a retail center?
faqs.a: Typically the trailing two years, which is usually enough to tell whether turnover is a one-time event or a pattern tied to the center's tenant mix.
